Done.

What I set up
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, track=canary
  - container name/port: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)

- Service update: recommendation-engine (ClusterIP)
  - selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both stable (version=v2.0) and canary (track=canary)
  - ports preserved: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Verification
- Pods (2 stable + 2 canary) are Running:
  - engine-v2-0-... x2 (labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0)
  - engine-v2-1-... x2 (labels: app=recommendation-engine, track=canary)
- Service Endpoints now include all 4 pods on port 8080, so traffic will be roughly 50/50 across stable and canary due to equal number of endpoints.

Notes and rollbacks
- For ~50% traffic, keep equal replica counts across stable and canary. Adjust replicas to bias traffic (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary).
- Roll back to 0% canary by either:
  - Setting the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or
  - Scaling engine-v2-1 to 0 replicas or deleting the canary Deployment.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I set up
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, track=canary
  - container name/port: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)

- Service update: recommendation-engine (ClusterIP)
  - selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both stable (version=v2.0) and canary (track=canary)
  - ports preserved: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Verification
- Pods (2 stable + 2 canary) are Running:
  - engine-v2-0-... x2 (labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0)
  - engine-v2-1-... x2 (labels: app=recommendation-engine, track=canary)
- Service Endpoints now include all 4 pods on port 8080, so traffic will be roughly 50/50 across stable and canary due to equal number of endpoints.

Notes and rollbacks
- For ~50% traffic, keep equal replica counts across stable and canary. Adjust replicas to bias traffic (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary).
- Roll back to 0% canary by either:
  - Setting the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or
  - Scaling engine-v2-1 to 0 replicas or deleting the canary Deployment.

outputSteps.content:
I found the crash was caused by an invalid startup command in the Deployment (command=/bin/sh -c with args=nonexistent_command), which put the pod into CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so the container starts with the image’s default command.
- Set imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent and defined containerPort 8080 (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080).
- Recreated the Deployment to ensure the bad command/args were fully cleared.

Result
- New pod is running: app-6df8647c78-w4nlr, 1/1 Ready, Running.
- Warning events you might see are from the previous failed pods; the current one is healthy.

Want me to expose it?
- I can create a Service (ClusterIP/LoadBalancer) or set up a quick port-forward for testing.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass named “sc,” so the volume couldn’t be provisioned.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC with the default StorageClass “standard” (no data loss risk since the PVC was never bound).

Result
- The pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and the container is Ready.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass named “sc,” so the volume couldn’t be provisioned.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC with the default StorageClass “standard” (no data loss risk since the PVC was never bound).

Result
- The pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and the container is Ready.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

I fixed it.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass named “sc,” so the volume couldn’t be provisioned.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC with the default StorageClass “standard” (no data loss risk since the PVC was never bound).

Result
- The pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and the container is Ready.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed the webapp in the orders namespace.

Root cause
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 (not 80) and doesn’t serve /get_status or /is_ready. Your Deployment’s probes were hitting non-existent paths on port 80, keeping pods unready. The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic couldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readiness/liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service:
  - Updated targetPort to 8080 (service still on port 80).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Ready and Running (webapp-b8996969f-slqqv).
- Endpoints: healthy and pointing to the pod on port 8080.
- Probes are succeeding (200 responses).

How to verify
- Port-forward and curl:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - curl http://127.0.0.1:8080  (should return the default Nginx page)

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress/Route.
- If you prefer custom health paths, add them to the app and I’ll update the probes accordingly.
- Want me to scale replicas up from 1?

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I investigated and fixed the webapp in the orders namespace.

Root cause
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 (not 80) and doesn’t serve /get_status or /is_ready. Your Deployment’s probes were hitting non-existent paths on port 80, keeping pods unready. The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic couldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readiness/liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service:
  - Updated targetPort to 8080 (service still on port 80).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Ready and Running (webapp-b8996969f-slqqv).
- Endpoints: healthy and pointing to the pod on port 8080.
- Probes are succeeding (200 responses).

How to verify
- Port-forward and curl:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - curl http://127.0.0.1:8080  (should return the default Nginx page)

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress/Route.
- If you prefer custom health paths, add them to the app and I’ll update the probes accordingly.
- Want me to scale replicas up from 1?

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed the webapp in the orders namespace.

Root cause
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 (not 80) and doesn’t serve /get_status or /is_ready. Your Deployment’s probes were hitting non-existent paths on port 80, keeping pods unready. The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic couldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readiness/liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service:
  - Updated targetPort to 8080 (service still on port 80).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Ready and Running (webapp-b8996969f-slqqv).
- Endpoints: healthy and pointing to the pod on port 8080.
- Probes are succeeding (200 responses).

How to verify
- Port-forward and curl:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - curl http://127.0.0.1:8080  (should return the default Nginx page)

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress/Route.
- If you prefer custom health paths, add them to the app and I’ll update the probes accordingly.
- Want me to scale replicas up from 1?

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- Your Role pod-reader-role only granted list on deployments.apps, not on pods. The RoleBinding correctly bound the service account, but it didn’t have pod permissions to use.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant get, list, watch on core API pods.

You can verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- Or try: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- Your Role pod-reader-role only granted list on deployments.apps, not on pods. The RoleBinding correctly bound the service account, but it didn’t have pod permissions to use.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant get, list, watch on core API pods.

You can verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- Or try: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding instead.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- Your Role pod-reader-role only granted list on deployments.apps, not on pods. The RoleBinding correctly bound the service account, but it didn’t have pod permissions to use.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant get, list, watch on core API pods.

You can verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- Or try: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Service selector mismatch: Service web/nginx was selecting app=web, but the Deployment and Pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: Endpoints for the Service were empty, so traffic had nowhere to go.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080. The Service was targeting port 80, so even if endpoints were selected, it would have targeted the wrong port.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx (was app=web)
  - targetPort: 8080 (was 80)
- After the change, Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.39:8080

Verification
- Service endpoints now show the backing Pod:
  - kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx → 10.244.0.39:8080
- In-cluster HTTP check returned 200 OK:
  - From a test pod: wget -qO- -S --spider http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - Response: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible inside the cluster. If you need external access, we can:
  - Change Service type to NodePort or LoadBalancer, or
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller). Tell me the hostname/path you want and I’ll set it up.

Optional cleanup
- I left a test pod named nettool in namespace web for you to verify access:
  - kubectl -n web exec -it nettool -- sh -c "wget -qO- -S --spider http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local"
- You can remove it when done:
  - kubectl -n web delete pod nettool

If you want me to expose nginx externally, let me know your preferred method (NodePort/LoadBalancer/Ingress and hostname) and I’ll configure it.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Service selector mismatch: Service web/nginx was selecting app=web, but the Deployment and Pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: Endpoints for the Service were empty, so traffic had nowhere to go.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080. The Service was targeting port 80, so even if endpoints were selected, it would have targeted the wrong port.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx (was app=web)
  - targetPort: 8080 (was 80)
- After the change, Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.39:8080

Verification
- Service endpoints now show the backing Pod:
  - kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx → 10.244.0.39:8080
- In-cluster HTTP check returned 200 OK:
  - From a test pod: wget -qO- -S --spider http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - Response: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible inside the cluster. If you need external access, we can:
  - Change Service type to NodePort or LoadBalancer, or
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller). Tell me the hostname/path you want and I’ll set it up.

Optional cleanup
- I left a test pod named nettool in namespace web for you to verify access:
  - kubectl -n web exec -it nettool -- sh -c "wget -qO- -S --spider http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local"

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Service selector mismatch: Service web/nginx was selecting app=web, but the Deployment and Pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: Endpoints for the Service were empty, so traffic had nowhere to go.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080. The Service was targeting port 80, so even if endpoints were selected, it would have targeted the wrong port.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx (was app=web)
  - targetPort: 8080 (was 80)
- After the change, Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.39:8080

Verification
- Service endpoints now show the backing Pod:
  - kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx → 10.244.0.39:8080
- In-cluster HTTP check returned 200 OK:
  - From a test pod: wget -qO- -S --spider http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - Response: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible inside the cluster. If you need external access, we can:
  - Change Service type to NodePort or LoadBalancer, or
  - Create an Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller). Tell me the hostname/path you want and I’ll set it up.

Optional cleanup
- I left a test pod named nettool in namespace web for you to verify access:
  - kubectl -n web exec -it nettool -- sh -c "wget -qO- -S --spider http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local"
- You can remove it when done:
  - kubectl -n web delete pod nettool

If you want me to expose nginx externally, let me know your preferred method (NodePort/LoadBalancer/Ingress and hostname) and I’ll configure it.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but no nodes in the cluster have that label. Scheduler events showed “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector,” leaving all pods Pending. With no running pods, the Service had no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Pods (before): 0/1 Pending with FailedScheduling due to nodeSelector.
  - Nodes: none labeled environment=production-gpu.
  - Service Endpoints: empty.

Fix applied
- I updated the web-app-deployment in namespace webshop-frontend to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule onto the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running
  - Service Endpoints: 10.244.0.44:80, 10.244.0.45:80 (populated)

Current state
- Deployment: web-app-deployment (2 replicas), image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-rc4cc (Running, 10.244.0.44)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-b29qb (Running, 10.244.0.45)
- Service: web-app-service now has endpoints and should accept connections.

How to verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- In-cluster test:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -c "curl -sI web-app-service"
  - Expect HTTP 200/301/302 from nginx

Notes and options
- If the app truly must run on GPU/“production-gpu” nodes, label the appropriate node(s) (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu) and then reintroduce the nodeSelector.
- Consider adding readiness probes so the Service only routes to ready pods.
- Prefer a fixed image tag instead of latest to avoid surprise changes.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but no nodes in the cluster have that label. Scheduler events showed “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector,” leaving all pods Pending. With no running pods, the Service had no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Pods (before): 0/1 Pending with FailedScheduling due to nodeSelector.
  - Nodes: none labeled environment=production-gpu.
  - Service Endpoints: empty.

Fix applied
- I updated the web-app-deployment in namespace webshop-frontend to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule onto the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running
  - Service Endpoints: 10.244.0.44:80, 10.244.0.45:80 (populated)

Current state
- Deployment: web-app-deployment (2 replicas), image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-rc4cc (Running, 10.244.0.44)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-b29qb (Running, 10.244.0.45)
- Service: web-app-service now has endpoints and should accept connections.

How to verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- In-cluster test:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -c "curl -sI web-app-service"
  - Expect HTTP 200/301/302 from nginx

Notes and options
- If the app truly must run on GPU/“production-gpu” nodes, label the appropriate node(s) (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu) and then reintroduce the nodeSelector.
- Consider adding readiness probes so the Service only routes to ready pods.
- Prefer a fixed image tag instead of latest to avoid surprise changes.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but no nodes in the cluster have that label. Scheduler events showed “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector,” leaving all pods Pending. With no running pods, the Service had no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Pods (before): 0/1 Pending with FailedScheduling due to nodeSelector.
  - Nodes: none labeled environment=production-gpu.
  - Service Endpoints: empty.

Fix applied
- I updated the web-app-deployment in namespace webshop-frontend to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule onto the available node.
- Result:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running
  - Service Endpoints: 10.244.0.44:80, 10.244.0.45:80 (populated)

Current state
- Deployment: web-app-deployment (2 replicas), image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-rc4cc (Running, 10.244.0.44)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-b29qb (Running, 10.244.0.45)
- Service: web-app-service now has endpoints and should accept connections.

How to verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
- In-cluster test:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -c "curl -sI web-app-service"
  - Expect HTTP 200/301/302 from nginx

Notes and options
- If the app truly must run on GPU/“production-gpu” nodes, label the appropriate node(s) (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu) and then reintroduce the nodeSelector.
- Consider adding readiness probes so the Service only routes to ready pods.
- Prefer a fixed image tag instead of latest to avoid surprise changes.

I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant dev environment. Highlights and what’s been applied:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding ns-admin in each dev namespace binding ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice → dev-alice, bob → dev-bob, charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readers in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod: no RBAC granted to developers (only cluster-admins can access)

Service accounts
- Created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Each SA has admin on its own namespace and view on dev-shared (via bindings above)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - cpu requests: 2, cpu limits: 2
  - memory requests: 4Gi, memory limits: 4Gi
  - pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu requests: 4, cpu limits: 4
  - memory requests: 8Gi, memory limits: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu requests: 8, cpu limits: 8
  - memory requests: 16Gi, memory limits: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (ingress and egress) enforced in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Intra-namespace communication allowed (pods can talk to pods in the same namespace)
- DNS/system services allowed: egress to kube-system from all user/stage/prod namespaces
- Dev access scoping:
  - dev-{alice,bob,charlie} egress allowed to dev-shared
  - dev-shared ingress allows traffic only from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (and from dev-shared itself)
  - No cross-developer traffic (e.g., dev-alice <-> dev-bob/charlie blocked)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace ingress allowed; egress restricted to same namespace and kube-system
  - No dev namespace can reach staging/prod, and staging/prod cannot reach dev

Notes and next steps
- The User subjects “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” assume your cluster’s auth maps those identities (e.g., via OIDC or client cert CN). If their subject names differ, tell me and I’ll adjust the RoleBindings.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net). Verify your CNI supports NetworkPolicy.
- If you prefer stricter least-privilege than ClusterRole admin in dev namespaces (e.g., disallow managing Roles/RoleBindings), I can switch to custom Roles with only the verbs/resources you want.
- For better quota effectiveness, consider adding LimitRanges to set default requests/limits in each namespace.

If you want, I can export the full YAML bundle or run quick connectivity tests (e.g., deploy a test pod and curl between namespaces) to validate the policies.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant dev environment. Highlights and what’s been applied:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding ns-admin in each dev namespace binding ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice → dev-alice, bob → dev-bob, charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readers in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod: no RBAC granted to developers (only cluster-admins can access)

Service accounts
- Created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Each SA has admin on its own namespace and view on dev-shared (via bindings above)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - cpu requests: 2, cpu limits: 2
  - memory requests: 4Gi, memory limits: 4Gi
  - pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu requests: 4, cpu limits: 4
  - memory requests: 8Gi, memory limits: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu requests: 8, cpu limits: 8
  - memory requests: 16Gi, memory limits: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (ingress and egress) enforced in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Intra-namespace communication allowed (pods can talk to pods in the same namespace)
- DNS/system services allowed: egress to kube-system from all user/stage/prod namespaces
- Dev access scoping:
  - dev-{alice,bob,charlie} egress allowed to dev-shared
  - dev-shared ingress allows traffic only from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (and from dev-shared itself)
  - No cross-developer traffic (e.g., dev-alice <-> dev-bob/charlie blocked)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace ingress allowed; egress restricted to same namespace and kube-system
  - No dev namespace can reach staging/prod, and staging/prod cannot reach dev

Notes and next steps
- The User subjects “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” assume your cluster’s auth maps those identities (e.g., via OIDC or client cert CN). If their subject names differ, tell me and I’ll adjust the RoleBindings.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net). Verify your CNI supports NetworkPolicy.
- If you prefer stricter least-privilege than ClusterRole admin in dev namespaces (e.g., disallow managing Roles/RoleBindings), I can switch to custom Roles with only the verbs/resources you want.
- For better quota effectiveness, consider adding LimitRanges to set default requests/limits in each namespace.

If you want, I can export the full YAML bundle or run quick connectivity tests (e.g., deploy a test pod and curl between namespaces) to validate the policies.

I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant dev environment. Highlights and what’s been applied:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding ns-admin in each dev namespace binding ClusterRole admin to:
    - User: alice → dev-alice, bob → dev-bob, charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readers in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod: no RBAC granted to developers (only cluster-admins can access)

Service accounts
- Created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Each SA has admin on its own namespace and view on dev-shared (via bindings above)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - cpu requests: 2, cpu limits: 2
  - memory requests: 4Gi, memory limits: 4Gi
  - pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu requests: 4, cpu limits: 4
  - memory requests: 8Gi, memory limits: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu requests: 8, cpu limits: 8
  - memory requests: 16Gi, memory limits: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (ingress and egress) enforced in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Intra-namespace communication allowed (pods can talk to pods in the same namespace)
- DNS/system services allowed: egress to kube-system from all user/stage/prod namespaces
- Dev access scoping:
  - dev-{alice,bob,charlie} egress allowed to dev-shared
  - dev-shared ingress allows traffic only from dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (and from dev-shared itself)
  - No cross-developer traffic (e.g., dev-alice <-> dev-bob/charlie blocked)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace ingress allowed; egress restricted to same namespace and kube-system
  - No dev namespace can reach staging/prod, and staging/prod cannot reach dev

Notes and next steps
- The User subjects “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” assume your cluster’s auth maps those identities (e.g., via OIDC or client cert CN). If their subject names differ, tell me and I’ll adjust the RoleBindings.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net). Verify your CNI supports NetworkPolicy.
- If you prefer stricter least-privilege than ClusterRole admin in dev namespaces (e.g., disallow managing Roles/RoleBindings), I can switch to custom Roles with only the verbs/resources you want.
- For better quota effectiveness, consider adding LimitRanges to set default requests/limits in each namespace.

If you want, I can export the full YAML bundle or run quick connectivity tests (e.g., deploy a test pod and curl between namespaces) to validate the policies.

rawInput.resource:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: statefulset-test
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: statefulset-test
  labels:
    app: db
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: db
  ports:
    - name: dummy
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: statefulset-test
spec:
  replicas: 3
  serviceName: db
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: init-data
          image: busybox:1.36
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              set -eu
              if [ ! -f /data/test ]; then
                printf 'initial_data' > /data/test
              fi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      containers:
        - name: main
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep infinity"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 1Gi

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: statefulset-test
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: statefulset-test
  labels:
    app: db
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: db
  ports:
    - name: dummy
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: statefulset-test
spec:
  replicas: 3
  serviceName: db
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: init-data
          image: busybox:1.36
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              set -eu
              if [ ! -f /data/test ]; then
                printf 'initial_data' > /data/test
              fi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      containers:
        - name: main
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep infinity"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 1Gi
